title: How to Raise Capital for a Real Estate Syndication: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Raising capital for a real estate syndication doesn't have to be intimidating. This guide walks you through exactly how to attract investors, structure your deal, and close your first syndication with confidence.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to raise capital for a real estate syndication
metaDescription: Learn how to raise capital for a real estate syndication with proven strategies, legal tips, and step-by-step guidance for new and experienced investors.

sections.content: Real estate syndications let everyday investors pool money together to buy larger properties they couldn't afford alone. An apartment complex, a shopping center, a self-storage facility — these are the kinds of deals that build serious wealth. But first, you need capital. And unless you have millions sitting in the bank, that means learning how to raise money from other people. If you've ever wondered how to raise capital for a real estate syndication, this guide breaks it all down in plain, practical language.
What Is a Real Estate Syndication?

A real estate syndication is a partnership between a sponsor (also called the general partner or GP) and a group of passive investors (limited partners or LPs). The sponsor finds the deal, manages the project, and makes day-to-day decisions. The investors provide most of the capital in exchange for a share of the profits. A typical syndication might involve one sponsor raising $2 million from 20 investors at $100,000 each to buy a $7 million apartment building, with the remaining $5 million covered by a commercial loan. It's a powerful model — if you execute it correctly.
Step 1: Get Your Legal Structure Right Before You Raise a Dime

Before you approach a single investor, you need to understand securities law. In the United States, raising capital from investors — even friends and family — is regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Most syndications operate under Regulation D, specifically Rule 506(b) or Rule 506(c). Under 506(b), you can raise from up to 35 non-accredited investors and unlimited accredited investors, but you cannot publicly advertise. Under 506(c), you can advertise publicly, but all investors must be accredited (meaning they earn over $200,000 per year or have a net worth over $1 million excluding their primary home). Hire a securities attorney before you do anything else. Expect to pay between $5,000 and $15,000 for a proper private placement memorandum (PPM) and operating agreement. This is not an area to cut corners.

Pro Tip: Start building your investor list long before you have a deal under contract. Relationships take time. Most experienced syndicators say it takes 6 to 12 months of consistent relationship-building before investors are ready to write a check.
Step 2: Build Your Investor Network

Your investor network is your most valuable asset as a syndicator. Most first-time syndicators raise their initial capital from people they already know — friends, family, colleagues, and professional contacts. Start by making a list of everyone in your life who might have capital to invest. You're looking for people who are financially comfortable, interested in passive income, and trust you enough to invest with you. Don't overlook doctors, dentists, attorneys, and business owners. These professionals often earn high incomes but don't have time to actively manage real estate investments.
Where to Meet New Investors

items: Local real estate investment clubs and REIA meetings
LinkedIn — especially in groups focused on passive investing and wealth building
Podcasts and YouTube channels where you can demonstrate your expertise
Masterminds and real estate conferences like Best Ever Conference or IMN
Referrals from existing investors after your first successful deal

sections.content: Step 3: Create a Track Record (Even If You're New)

One of the biggest fears new syndicators face is the chicken-and-egg problem: investors want a track record, but you need investors to build one. Here's how to break through. If you're new to syndication but have experience in real estate — even as a wholesaler or flipper — document it. Investors care about your ability to find deals, manage risk, and deliver returns. You can also partner with a more experienced syndicator on your first deal. Taking a smaller slice of the GP equity in exchange for deal-finding or investor relations work is a common and smart way to get started. If you're brand new to real estate entirely, check out our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) to build your foundation first.

"Your first syndication won't be your best deal. But it will be the most important one — because it proves to the market, and to yourself, that you can execute." — Common wisdom among experienced syndicators
Step 4: Underwrite Deals That Investors Actually Want

Investors aren't going to hand you money based on enthusiasm alone. You need to present a compelling, well-underwritten deal with realistic projections. Most syndication investors look for a preferred return of 6% to 8% annually, an equity multiple of 1.5x to 2x over the hold period, and an IRR (internal rate of return) of 12% to 18%. These numbers need to be backed by solid market research and conservative assumptions. Don't model 5% annual rent growth in a flat market just to make the numbers look good — sophisticated investors will spot it immediately and lose trust in you.

When evaluating potential syndication markets, focus on areas with strong population growth, job diversification, and landlord-friendly laws. Markets like [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) have consistently attracted syndication capital due to their growth fundamentals and strong rental demand. Step 5: Communicate Like a Pro
What Your Investor Pitch Should Include

items: Executive summary: property details, location, and investment thesis in one page
Market overview: why this city and submarket, backed by data
Deal financials: purchase price, renovation budget, projected NOI, and exit strategy
Return projections: preferred return, equity split, projected IRR and equity multiple
Your team: who's managing the property, who's on your legal and accounting team
Risk factors: be honest about what could go wrong and how you plan to mitigate it
How to invest: minimum investment amount, timeline, and wire instructions

sections.content: Transparency builds trust. Investors who feel informed — even about risks — are far more likely to invest again on your next deal. Set up a simple investor portal or even a shared Google Drive folder where LPs can access monthly updates, financials, and distribution notices. Regular communication turns one-time investors into repeat partners.
Step 6: Structure the Deal Fairly

A fair deal structure keeps investors happy and builds your reputation. The most common structure is an 70/30 or 80/20 split, with LPs receiving the larger share. Investors also typically receive a preferred return (say, 7%) before the GP takes any profit split. Some deals include a waterfall structure where the GP's percentage increases after hitting certain return thresholds. If you're learning the basics of deal structure from the ground up, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) covers key concepts around deal analysis that apply across all real estate strategies.

Pro Tip: Never promise a specific return. SEC regulations prohibit guarantee language in investor communications. Instead, use projected or estimated figures and always present your assumptions clearly.
How Long Does It Take to Raise Capital?

First-time syndicators typically take 30 to 90 days to fully fund a deal once it's under contract. Having a strong investor list built in advance dramatically shortens this timeline. Some experienced syndicators with an established investor base can fully fund a deal in 48 to 72 hours. To get there, you need to consistently add value to your audience — through newsletters, deal updates, market analysis, and educational content — long before you need their money. Common Mistakes to Avoid

items: Raising money before having legal documents in place — this is a securities violation
Overpromising returns to attract investors and then underdelivering
Underestimating capital expenses and renovation costs, wiping out investor returns
Not vetting investors — make sure they understand the risks and meet accreditation requirements
Skipping the PPM to save money — this document protects both you and your investors
Failing to communicate after the money is raised — radio silence destroys investor relationships
